elements.visible_text: Building & Public Works
Sector Cyber Resilience & Credit Intelligence
Migrated edition - evidence as of 14 October 2026; no research update
Report period: 1 September 2025 to 14 October 2026
Geographical scope: global, primary focus EU, EEA and UK; North America and Asia for comparison
Evidence cut-off: 14 October 2026
Classification: not specified in source edition
Version: 1.0-M (migrated from the baseline seven-slide edition)

slides.label: Executive Sector Risk Snapshot
slides.headline: Building & Public Works shows provisional High cyber and third-party exposure that reaches lenders mainly through contractor liquidity; fraud and governance cannot be assessed from the source edition.

rows: Only cyber-enabled payment fraud covered (one police alert); wider fraud (Q10) not covered
176 of 1,140 industrial ransomware claims in Q2 2026; third of all sectors over 12 months
Best-documented disruptions spread through shared owner IT and a public-sector supplier
Q13 not covered; one auditor finding at a public owner is not sector evidence

elements.visible_text: Key sector messages: (1) shared digital layers are the best-documented propagation pathway; (2) time-sensitive site operations turn IT outages into schedule loss; (3) regulation reaches construction indirectly through owners, procurement, product and data rules.
Threat direction: rising in cross-sector leak-site counts (industrial claims up 12% quarter on quarter; all-sector victims up 24.9% year on year); no construction-specific baseline exists.

Most consequential credit implications: owner payment constraint and programme delay strain contractor working capital; construction leads company insolvency counts in England and Wales (a count, not a rate).
Provisional ratings: no approved rubric; cross-sector comparison (Q14): not covered in source edition; confidence capped at Medium; public-owner cases over-represented.

slides.label: Sector Anatomy: Key Operations & Dependencies
slides.headline: Contractors depend on owner approvals and payments, shared project platforms on third-party cloud, ERP-reliant materials suppliers and exposed public-works OT - each a potential single point of failure.

rows: Planning consent, repairs ordering, supplier payment
One shared IT estate served three London boroughs
One supplier served a majority of Swedish municipalities
One platform: 17,850 customers hosted on third-party cloud
Supplier tier repeatedly targeted by ransomware
Many small operators with internet-exposed controllers
table.legacy_source: Ch1 subsector table; Ch6 dependency chains

elements.visible_text: Subsectors in scope: construction companies, civil engineering, public works, engineering and project management, building materials, construction technology, building automation and public project owners. Only dependencies evidenced in the source edition are shown.
elements.legacy_source: Report header; Ch1 subsector coverage; Ch6

elements.visible_text: A failure at an owner or shared platform stops several firms at once: the best-documented case halted planning for about 15 weeks.
Ask which owners, platforms and suppliers a borrower depends on, and whether it could value, certify and invoice without them.
Substitutability, bottleneck depth and platform market shares were not assessed in the source edition; no in-period building-automation incident was identified.

slides.label: Geopolitical Cyber Threat Outlook
slides.headline: Geopolitical exposure is evidenced only in fragments: exposed public-works OT faces state-linked pressure, while construction firms are more likely collateral than primary targets.

rows: Authority judged Iranian cyber retaliation very likely after Feb 2026 strikes; malicious activity at more than 30 Minnesota water systems (Jul 2026)
Bulletin is an estimative judgement; state made no attribution; media-reported Iran link is unconfirmed
Bremanger dam outflow valves opened for about four hours (Apr 2025)
Security service linked it to Russian methods (Aug 2025); contextual
Weak passwords and poor IT/OT separation

elements.visible_text: Source edition fragments: one national threat bulletin, two state statements, one regulator notice and one owner statement; no conflict-driven campaign against construction firms was documented.
State-linked intent towards poorly secured infrastructure reaches the public-works assets that contractors build, operate and maintain.
For public-works and infrastructure borrowers, ask about OT inventory, removal of internet exposure and IT/OT segregation.
Not covered in source edition: dedicated geopolitical analysis (Q07), exposed-region view and conflict-driven supply-chain exposure; attribution is preliminary or contextual.
Sources: S-001, S-012, S-013, S-017, S-025 (Tier 1); S-018 (Tier 2); S-014 (Tier 3) - Period: Apr 2025-Oct 2026

elements.visible_text: Owner-side and supplier incidents disrupt the consents, instructions and payments that contractors depend on, even when the contractor itself is not attacked.
Treat owner digital disruption as foreseeable in contractor cash-flow and contract planning.
Second and third detailed case studies: not covered in source edition. No contractor disclosed cost or delay; developments after 14 Oct 2026: not covered in source edition.

slides.label: Control Weaknesses & Resilience Priorities
slides.headline: Documented weaknesses cluster in identity, segregation and monitoring; six priorities address the evidenced threat patterns.

rows: Single shared estates and SaaS platforms (Kensington and Chelsea, Miljödata)
VPN without MFA, unpatched edge and backup (Akira); human error (Kensington and Chelsea)
A3 Segregate OT and site systems
Weak passwords, poor IT/OT separation (Bremanger); 81% of OT cases with weak segmentation
Supplier email compromise and bank-detail replacement
Owner duties under NIS2, CER and procurement rules
Time-sensitive operations stopped by IT loss (Femern, media-reported)

elements.visible_text: Documented weaknesses: human error and a fragmented legacy estate; missing software checks and real-time monitoring; weak passwords and poor IT/OT separation; VPNs without MFA and unpatched backup servers.
elements.legacy_source: Ch5 mechanism; Ch2 incidents; Ch2 advisory

elements.visible_text: The same few weaknesses enable both ransomware and OT manipulation, so a small set of capabilities prevents or contains most evidenced disruption.
Use the priorities as discussion topics with borrowers; they are not a control audit or compliance finding.
Confidence reflects source-edition claim confidence; no control-effectiveness data for any firm exist in the source edition.

slides.label: Regulatory & Supervisory Resilience Expectations
slides.headline: Construction sits outside the direct scope of EU and UK cyber-resilience law; obligations reach contractors through owners, procurement, product and data rules, and US coverage is comparative only.

rows: Binding via national law; 4 Member States referred (Jul 2026)
Not a listed sector; owner duties flow down
Binding via national law; identification due 17 Jul 2026
Designated operators may impose resilience terms
Breach notification and fines across the chain
Cyber and security-of-supply terms in tenders
Could reach MSPs and designated suppliers
Disclosure within four business days of materiality

elements.visible_text: Consequences of non-compliance in the source edition: penalties requested against four Member States; GDPR fines of SEK 1.8m (Miljödata) and GBP 4.4m (Interserve, historical).
In-period pressure: CRA reporting began, CER identification fell due and an EU procurement reform with cyber terms was proposed.
Check that project and guarantee documentation reflects owner-imposed cyber and notification terms.
Not covered in source edition: US sector cyber rules beyond SEC disclosure, supervisory priorities and national NIS2 scope extensions.
Sources: S-030, S-032 to S-042, S-046, S-047 (Tier 1) - Period: legal milestones 2016-2027; status at 14 Oct 2026

slides.label: Financial Impact of Cyber Incidents
slides.headline: Public financial evidence is thin and cannot be added up; the evidence suggests time - weeks of site downtime and months of owner disruption - is the main cost driver.

rows: Kensington and Chelsea revenues and benefits outage
Interserve fine; recovery and advisory fees

elements.visible_text: In-period quantified outcomes come from one public owner and one regulator; no contractor or supplier disclosed a cyber-driven cost, delay or contractual effect.
Values differ in currency, statistic type and population and are never summed; no sector loss estimate is produced.
Focus on duration and liquidity: how long a borrower could operate and collect cash without key systems or owner payments.
Absence of disclosure is a gap, not evidence of zero loss; ransom payments and multi-year trends are not covered in source edition.

slides.label: Cyber-to-Credit Risk Transmission & Stress Scenarios
slides.headline: Cyber disruption reaches debt service through delayed certification and payment, programme slippage and supplier default; duration evidence supports only part of the 1-, 4- and 8-week bands.
slides.banner: Illustrative - not a forecast or loss estimate

rows: Common dependency: shared platform or cloud availability failure
Multi-day outage; 77% tolerate no more than five days without project documentation
Targeted disruption: major contractor or public-works operator
Within the legacy one-to-four-week band; one US town reportedly restored a plant in about 90 minutes
Within the legacy band; ransomware downtime averaged about 24 days
Duration not evidenced for this mechanism; owner-side case restoration took about 15 weeks to six months

elements.visible_text: Transmission: disruption -> programme and site operations -> valuations and owner payments -> contractor cash flow and working capital -> margins and claims -> facility drawdown and debt service.

slides.label: Credit Officer Engagement: Key Questions & Actions
slides.headline: Five client discussion topics, with early-warning indicators and referral triggers, turn sector evidence into proportionate borrower engagement.

rows: Could you certify and invoice for 30 days without your main owners and platforms?
Reliance on one owner or platform without tested fallback
Is MFA on all remote access, with edge and backup systems patched?
New joint advisory on edge flaws
Are controllers off the internet and OT segregated from IT?
Are payment-detail changes confirmed out of band?
Which milestones would a one-to-four-week outage cross?
Incident notice on a major programme
Outage would cross a contractual milestone

elements.visible_text: Indicators also include leak-site claims above the Q2 2026 baseline of 176 construction claims per quarter, the UK bill, NIS2 court rulings, procurement adoption and first CRA reporting.
Practical resilience improvements: dependency mapping, MFA and patching, OT segregation, payment-change confirmation, contractual flow-down and tested fallback.
Proportionate next steps: raise the topics at review, record answers as self-reported, escalate to the Risk Committee when an indicator fires.
Topics are sector-informed priorities, not findings on any borrower's controls or creditworthiness; referral triggers are reframed from the source edition.
